explanations.answer: Go show love to her again
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The LORD says, “Go show love to your wife again…” (Hosea 3:1). Look at that word again. She is loved by another, and the LORD still sends Hosea to love her. I think that's a big ask, and Hosea is the one telling us about it.

explanations.answer: Let her go her own way
explanations.explanation: I get why that one tempts you, friend. Plenty of us would grab our hat and head out the door. But the LORD says, “Go show love to your wife again…” (Hosea 3:1). Hosea isn't told to let go. He's told to love.

explanations.answer: Send her back to her family
explanations.explanation: Her family never comes up in these verses. The LORD's words are, “Go show love to your wife again…” (Hosea 3:1). The job lands on Hosea himself, not on somebody else's front porch. Hosea is the one who goes.

Gods, yes. The LORD says to love her “…as the LORD loves the Israelites, though they turn to other gods…” (Hosea 3:1). That's the comparison. The Israelites turn to other gods, and the LORD loves them anyway.

Nations is a fair guess, friend, but that's not the word. The verse says they turn to other gods. It even adds that they “…love to offer raisin cakes to idols.” (Hosea 3:1). Raisins belong in my cookies, and those cookies never go to an idol.

Lands sounds like a good fit, but that's not the word. The LORD loves the Israelites “…though they turn to other gods…” (Hosea 3:1). It's about who they turn to, not where they go. One word changes the whole line.

He buys her, baker. Hosea says, “So I bought her for fifteen shekels of silver and a homer and a lethech of barley.” (Hosea 3:2). Silver and barley, so no coupons. Not even the expired coupon I shared a junk drawer with would have covered this one.

No courtroom anywhere in these verses, friend. No judge, no gavel, no lawyer in a loud tie. Hosea says, “So I bought her for fifteen shekels of silver and a homer and a lethech of barley.” (Hosea 3:2). He pays.

Sending a message sounds easy, doesn't it? But Hosea doesn't just send word. He says, “So I bought her for fifteen shekels of silver and a homer and a lethech of barley.” (Hosea 3:2). That's a real price, in silver and in barley.

Right, baker. Hosea tells her, “You must live with me for many days; you must not be promiscuous or belong to another…” (Hosea 3:3). Living with him and not belonging to another go together in that line. That's what he asks of her.
Her family never shows up in this verse, friend. Hosea tells her, “you must not be promiscuous or belong to another…” (Hosea 3:3). Those are the things he names. Visiting anybody isn't on his list.

No city limits in this verse, baker. Hosea doesn't talk about where she can go. He says, “you must not be promiscuous or belong to another…” (Hosea 3:3). That's what he asks of her for those many days.

Close, friend, but this one has a twist. Hosea does have rules for her, and then he says, “…and I will do the same for you.” (Hosea 3:3). So he makes a promise of his own. He puts himself in it too, and that changes how the whole verse sounds.

False is right, baker. Hosea tells her what to do, and then he adds, “…and I will do the same for you.” (Hosea 3:3). So he does make a promise of his own. It isn't a one-way deal, because he's in it with her.

That's it, baker. Hosea says the Israelites “…must live many days without king or prince…” (Hosea 3:4). Picture a job site with no boss and no manager. Nobody even to ask where the extension cord went.

Judges and generals sound official, but they're not in this verse, friend. Hosea says the Israelites “…must live many days without king or prince…” (Hosea 3:4). That's the first thing on his list. A judge and a general are nowhere on it.

That's a sneaky one, baker. Priest and prophet feel like they'd be on the list. But the verse says “…without king or prince…” (Hosea 3:4). The list goes on to name sacrifice, sacred pillar, ephod and idol, and no priest or prophet shows up.
Not this time, friend. The verse says the Israelites must live many days “…without ephod or idol.” (Hosea 3:4). So no ephod, and no idols either. They're on the without list, not the keep list.

False, baker, you read it right. Hosea says the Israelites “must live many days… without ephod or idol.” (Hosea 3:4). Both are gone from the picture. The idols are on the list of things they'll go without.

True, baker. Hosea says, “Afterward, the people of Israel will return and seek the LORD their God…” (Hosea 3:5). Look at that word afterward. The many days don't get the last word, and that's good news.

I think the many days might make this one tempting, friend. Without a king and without sacrifice, that sounds like a long stretch. But Hosea says, “Afterward, the people of Israel will return and seek the LORD their God…” (Hosea 3:5). So the answer is true, and the story turns toward return.

His goodness, baker. Hosea says, “They will come trembling to the LORD and to His goodness in the last days.” (Hosea 3:5). The text puts goodness right next to the trembling. And this is the last thing Hosea says in the passage.

Trembling and anger sound like they go together, friend. But that's not what the verse says. It says, “They will come trembling to the LORD and to His goodness in the last days.” (Hosea 3:5). Hosea ends on goodness.

A temple would fit the picture, but it isn't in this verse. Hosea says, “They will come trembling to the LORD and to His goodness in the last days.” (Hosea 3:5). The second thing they come to is His goodness. The verse doesn't name a building.
